note: Array holes (BLOCKER B2). A hole is not `undefined` stored at an index — it is the absence of the index, and the difference is exactly what breaks a canonicalizer: `Array.prototype.map` SKIPS holes rather than visiting them, so a writer built on map-then-join emits `[1,,3]`. Those bytes are not JSON; `JSON.parse` rejects them. The failure mode is therefore worse than a wrong digest — it is a document that seals, digests, signs, and can never be read back, and the refusal surfaces at whoever tries to parse it rather than at whoever produced it. JSON cannot spell a hole, so the cases are described and materialized by `canonical.test.ts`. Both a literal hole and `new Array(n)` are covered because they arrive from different code: a literal from hand-written data, `new Array(n)` from a preallocation that was never filled.

cases.name: literal-hole
cases.why: `[1, , 3]`: elements 0 and 2 present, index 1 absent. The first index that is not `in` the array is 1, so that is the index the refusal must name.

cases.name: preallocated
cases.why: `new Array(3)`: length 3, no indices at all. Every element is a hole, so the refusal names index 0 — the first one checked.

carriers.why: The same value has to be refused wherever it can reach a sealed document, so each case is canonicalized three ways: bare, as a tuple's profile-declared axis, and as a manifest's namespaced extension. A canonicalizer fixed only on the path someone happened to test is fixed on one path.
